mpesaSteps.title: Send Money
mpesaSteps.when: Paying a person: a friend, a driver, a small trader who gives you their phone number.
steps: Open the M-PESA app (or dial *334# / open the SIM Toolkit menu).
Choose Send Money.
Enter the recipient's phone number.
Enter the amount.
Enter your M-Pesa PIN and confirm.
Check the name shown in the confirmation before you finish, then wait for the SMS from MPESA.
mpesaSteps.example: Your boda rider says 'send to 0712 345 678'. Send KSh 200, check the name matches, and show him the SMS. Small traders may instead use Pochi la Biashara, which also works through Send Money.

mpesaSteps.title: Pay Bill
mpesaSteps.when: Paying a business or organisation that gives you a Paybill number and an account number: hotels, utilities, schools, some restaurants.
steps: Open the M-PESA app or menu and choose Lipa na M-PESA.
Choose Pay Bill.
Enter the business number (Paybill).
Enter the account number they gave you (often your name, room or invoice number).
Enter the amount and your PIN.
Check the business name on screen, confirm, and keep the SMS as your receipt.
mpesaSteps.example: Your guesthouse says 'Paybill 123456, account ROOM4'. Pay KSh 3,500 and show the SMS at reception.

mpesaSteps.title: Buy Goods (till number)
mpesaSteps.when: Paying in a shop, café, supermarket or petrol station that shows a 'Till Number' sign.
steps: Open the M-PESA app or menu and choose Lipa na M-PESA.
Choose Buy Goods and Services.
Enter the till number on the sign.
Enter the amount.
Enter your PIN, check the shop name and confirm.
Show the cashier your confirmation SMS.
mpesaSteps.example: A café sign says 'Till No. 987654'. Pay KSh 300 for your coffee; there is no account number to type.

mpesaSteps.title: Withdraw cash at an agent
mpesaSteps.when: You need cash. M-Pesa agents are small shops with a green M-PESA sign, found almost everywhere.
steps: Find an M-Pesa agent and tell them how much you want.
Open the M-PESA app or menu and choose Withdraw Cash, then From Agent.
Enter the agent number shown on their sign.
Enter the amount and your PIN.
Check the agent name, confirm, and show the agent your SMS.
Count your cash before you leave. The agent may ask for your ID.
mpesaSteps.example: You need KSh 2,000 for a market. Withdraw at the agent by your guesthouse; a small withdrawal fee comes out of your balance.

mpesaSteps.title: Pochi la Biashara
mpesaSteps.when: Paying a small trader (mama mboga, kiosk, tailor) who uses their personal phone number as a business wallet.
steps: Open the M-PESA app or menu and choose Lipa na M-PESA.
Choose Pochi la Biashara.
Enter the trader's phone number.
Enter the amount and your PIN.
Check the name and confirm.
mpesaSteps.example: A vegetable seller says 'Pochi, 0722 000 111'. Pay KSh 150 for tomatoes and onions.

mpesaFeesNote: These are rough fees for sending money to another registered M-Pesa user. Safaricom changes its tariffs from time to time, so check the current tariff on safaricom.co.ke or in the M-PESA app. Paying a shop by Buy Goods (till) is free for the customer; withdrawing cash at an agent has its own separate fees.

scams.title: Check notes for fakes
scams.body: Hold notes up to the light to see the watermark and security thread, and feel for raised print. Be extra careful with KSh 1,000 notes at night or in a hurry.

scams.title: The 'wrong send' M-Pesa trick
scams.body: Someone calls or texts saying they sent you money by mistake and asks you to send it back. Check your real M-Pesa balance and look for an SMS from 'MPESA' itself; never trust a forwarded or typed-out message. If a genuine error happened, Safaricom can reverse it, so tell them to contact Safaricom.

scams.title: Nobody genuine asks for your PIN
scams.body: Safaricom staff will never ask for your M-Pesa PIN over the phone or SMS. Hang up on callers who do, however official they sound. Safaricom's real customer care line is 100 (or 200 for postpay).

scams.title: Use ATMs on your own
scams.body: Choose ATMs inside banks, malls or supermarkets. Politely refuse 'helpers' at the machine, and cover the keypad when you type your PIN.

scams.title: Agree the fare first
scams.body: With street taxis, tuk-tuks and boda bodas, agree the price before you set off, or use an app so the fare is fixed.

scams.title: Check the name before you pay
scams.body: When you pay by M-Pesa, the confirmation screen shows the recipient's name. If it does not match the shop or person, cancel.

bargaining: Bargaining is normal at open markets, curio shops and with some street sellers.
Do not bargain in supermarkets, malls, chain cafés or anywhere with printed prices.
Smile, greet first ('Habari?') and keep it friendly; it is a conversation, not a fight.
At curio markets, opening at roughly half to two-thirds of the first price is common, but aim for a price that is fair to the seller.
Once you agree a price, stick to it and pay.
If the price does not work for you, say 'asante' and walk away politely.
bigNumbersNote: Prices in Uganda look huge because the Ugandan shilling has a low value per unit: roughly USh 3,600–3,800 to one US dollar, against about KSh 129 in Kenya, and coins are hardly used day to day. So a USh 10,000 note is only a few dollars. Quick trick: divide a Ugandan price by about 28–29 to get Kenyan shillings (exchange rates move, so treat this as a rough guide).
